title: User Mode and Kernel Mode
summary: Lesson 1.06 introduced the kernel as the part of Windows with full control of the hardware. This chapter looks inside. It starts with the boundary itself: the processor's **privilege levels**, what runs in **kernel mode** (the kernel, the HAL, drivers), how kernel memory is shared by all processes, and why code running there must be held to a far higher standard than anything in user mode.
markdown:
## Two privilege levels x64 processors have hardware **privilege levels**, called **rings**. Windows uses two: | Ring | Mode | What runs there | What it can do | |---|---|---|---| | 0 | **Kernel mode** | The Windows kernel, the hardware abstraction layer, device drivers | Everything: any memory, any instruction, the hardware | | 3 | **User mode** | Every application, including games and most services | Only its own address space; privileged instructions fault; hardware only through the kernel | The processor itself enforces the difference. In ring 3, instructions that control the hardware (disabling interrupts, loading page tables, talking to devices directly) cause an exception, and pages marked "supervisor only" in the page tables (lesson 6.02) cannot be touched. The only way up is a controlled gate: the **system call** (lesson 15.02). ## What lives in kernel mode ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph U["User mode (ring 3), one address space per process"] A["Applications"] S["Services"] N["ntdll.dll: system call stubs"] end subgraph K["Kernel mode (ring 0), one shared address space"] EX["Executive: object manager, memory manager,
I/O manager, process and thread manager, security"] KE["Kernel: scheduling, interrupts, synchronisation"] DR["Drivers: file systems, network, storage, graphics, USB ..."] WK["win32k.sys: windowing and graphics kernel side"] HAL["HAL: hardware abstraction layer"] end A --> N --> EX S --> N EX --> KE EX --> DR DR --> HAL KE --> HAL HAL --> HW["Hardware"] ``` - **ntoskrnl.exe** holds the **executive** (the managers this chapter covers: objects, memory, I/O, processes, security) and the **kernel** proper (scheduling, interrupts, low-level synchronisation). - **hal.dll**, the hardware abstraction layer, hides differences between motherboards and interrupt controllers. - **Drivers** (`.sys` files) are kernel modules: PE files like DLLs (lesson 9.02), loaded into kernel space, extending the kernel with support for devices and file systems. - **win32k.sys** is the kernel side of windows and graphics (lesson 5.05's messages are partly managed here). ## One kernel address space, shared by everything Lesson 6.02 showed each process's private lower half of the address space. The **upper half** is kernel space, and it is the **same** in every process: the kernel, every driver, and the kernel's data (the pools, lesson 15.04) are mapped at the same kernel addresses whichever process is running. Pages there are marked supervisor-only, so user code cannot touch them, but all kernel-mode code can touch all of it. That sharing is the key to the rest of this chapter: - A driver's global variable is one variable for the whole machine, not per process. - A driver writing through a bad pointer can corrupt the kernel, other drivers, or any process's data, because there is no boundary between kernel components. - There is no "this driver crashed, the rest carries on". An unhandled fault in kernel mode means the system cannot know what else is damaged, so Windows stops the machine with a **bug check** (the blue screen, lesson 15.07). ## The standard kernel code is held to In user mode, a crash ends one process and the operating system cleans up (lesson 1.06). In kernel mode: | User mode | Kernel mode | |---|---| | A crash ends the process | A crash stops the whole machine | | A leak is freed when the process exits | A leak lasts until reboot | | Bad pointers fault in your own space | Bad pointers can silently corrupt anything | | Many runtime libraries and C++ features available | A restricted environment: no standard library, careful exceptions, limited stack (lesson 16.02) | | Debug with Visual Studio on the same machine | Debug from a second machine or a VM's host (lesson 15.08) | That is why the rest of this course treats kernel work as something done **only in a virtual machine**, only with drivers you write for learning, with testing tools turned on, and why production drivers go through extensive testing and Microsoft's signing requirements (lesson 16.09). ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Thinking a driver is "like a DLL that runs as administrator" > It runs in ring 0 with the whole kernel's memory reachable. The rules, and the consequences of mistakes, are different. > [!warning] Assuming kernel globals are per process > Kernel space is shared; a driver's globals are machine-wide. > [!warning] Experimenting with kernel code on your main PC > Use a virtual machine you can restore (lesson 15.08). ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What runs in kernel mode on Windows? - Every program started by an administrator - Services, such as the print spooler and Windows Update + ntoskrnl, the HAL, device and file-system drivers, and win32k - ntdll.dll and kernel32.dll, which every program loads > Services and system DLLs run in user mode; ntdll only contains the stubs that make system calls. ? How does kernel address space differ from user address space? + The user half is per process; the kernel half is shared by all - The kernel has a separate physical computer's worth of memory - Each process has its own copy of the kernel - Kernel addresses are 32-bit and user addresses are 64-bit > One kernel serves every process, so its half of the address space is the same wherever you look. Only kernel-mode code can touch the kernel half. ? Name three ways kernel-mode mistakes are worse than user-mode ones. - They are harder to type, slower to compile, and need more comments - They show a dialog box, write a log, and close the program - They only appear in Release builds, on laptops and with antivirus installed + Crashes stop the whole machine, leaks last until reboot, and bad pointers can silently corrupt any part of the system > A user-mode crash ends one process; a kernel-mode crash ends everything. ? What enforces the separation between user mode and kernel mode? + The processor itself, by faulting privileged use - Windows checks every instruction in software - Nothing; programs promise to behave > Hardware privilege levels are the foundation. ? Why is the kernel half of the address space the same in every process? - Each process gets a copy of the kernel + One kernel serves the whole system, mapped alike - Kernel memory is not virtual > Supervisor-only pages keep user code out. ? Why does an unhandled fault in a driver stop the whole machine? - Drivers are always critical - Windows cannot restart drivers + Nothing in the kernel is walled off from it > Continuing could corrupt data, so Windows bug-checks. ```
ideas:
- Open **Task Manager → Details** and add the **Session** and **Platform** columns; then open **System Information** (`msinfo32`) → Software Environment → System Drivers to see the drivers loaded on your machine.
- Use Sysinternals Process Explorer, select the System process, and look at its threads: these are kernel threads.
- Read Microsoft's "Overview of Windows components" page in the driver documentation.

cards.q: What runs in kernel mode on Windows?
cards.a:
ntoskrnl, the HAL, device and file-system drivers, and win32k

Services and system DLLs run in user mode; ntdll only contains the stubs that make system calls.

cards.q: How does kernel address space differ from user address space?
cards.a:
The user half is per process; the kernel half is shared by all

One kernel serves every process, so its half of the address space is the same wherever you look. Only kernel-mode code can touch the kernel half.

cards.q: Name three ways kernel-mode mistakes are worse than user-mode ones.
cards.a:
Crashes stop the whole machine, leaks last until reboot, and bad pointers can silently corrupt any part of the system

A user-mode crash ends one process; a kernel-mode crash ends everything.

cards.q: What enforces the separation between user mode and kernel mode?
cards.a:
The processor itself, by faulting privileged use

Hardware privilege levels are the foundation.

cards.q: Why is the kernel half of the address space the same in every process?
cards.a:
One kernel serves the whole system, mapped alike

Supervisor-only pages keep user code out.

cards.q: Why does an unhandled fault in a driver stop the whole machine?
cards.a:
Nothing in the kernel is walled off from it

Continuing could corrupt data, so Windows bug-checks.
